# How to use this guide

Human Anatomy and Physiology II continues where Part I (BP101T) stopped. Part I covered cells, tissues, skin, bones, blood, the peripheral nervous system, special senses and the heart; this part covers the **brain and spinal cord, digestion, breathing, the kidneys, the endocrine glands, reproduction and basic genetics**. Like Part I it is a "draw and explain" subject: a neat labelled diagram, a clear flow chart of a mechanism and correct normal values earn most of the marks.

Study one unit at a time: read the notes, redraw every text diagram from memory on rough paper, learn the tables of normal values, attempt the question bank before reading the model answers, then finish with the unit's MCQs.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly; none has been split or joined. Units 3 and 5 each hold two syllabus topics (respiratory + urinary, reproductive + genetics), so their notes are divided into Part A and Part B. Where a syllabus topic overlaps Part I (the neuron, the autonomic control of organs), the notes give only what this syllabus adds and point back to BP101T. The syllabus writes "creatinine phosphate" under energetics; the notes explain that the energy store is creatine phosphate and creatinine is its waste product. The 16 practical guides follow the BP207P practical list.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it (some use 10 two-mark questions in Section A, or 5 of 7 seven-mark questions in Section C).

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long essays (10 marks), short answers (5 marks) and very short answers (2 marks, useful for class tests, sessionals and two-mark Section A papers).

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a diagram and normal values.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Nervous system and CNS | Action potential, synapse and synaptic transmission, neurotransmitters, classification of nerve fibres, CSF formation and circulation, parts of the brain with functions of cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla, spinal cord tracts, reflex arc |
| 2 Digestive system and energetics | Anatomy and functions of stomach, HCl secretion and its regulation, phases of gastric secretion, liver (structure and functions), pancreas, salivary glands, digestion and absorption of carbohydrate, protein and fat, peptic ulcer, ATP and BMR |
| 3 Respiratory and urinary system | Mechanism and regulation of respiration, lung volumes and capacities, transport of O2 and CO2, artificial respiration and CPR, structure of nephron, physiology of urine formation, micturition reflex, RAS, acid–base role of kidney |
| 4 Endocrine system | Classification and mechanism of hormone action (cAMP), pituitary hormones, thyroid hormone synthesis and disorders, PTH and calcium, adrenal cortex and medulla with Cushing's and Addison's, insulin and diabetes |
| 5 Reproduction and genetics | Male and female reproductive organs with diagrams, menstrual cycle, spermatogenesis and oogenesis, fertilization, pregnancy and parturition, sex hormones, DNA structure, protein synthesis, Mendelian and X-linked inheritance |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Put a diagram in every long answer, even if the question does not ask for one: neuron, action potential graph, synapse, sagittal section of brain, cross-section of spinal cord, reflex arc, stomach, villus, liver lobule, respiratory tract, spirogram, O2 dissociation curve, kidney section, nephron, pituitary with portal system, thyroid follicle, adrenal zones, testis and seminiferous tubule, female reproductive organs, menstrual cycle chart, sperm, DNA double helix. Label at least six parts with straight lines.
2. Begin with a one-line definition, then a flow chart for any mechanism: HCl secretion, regulation of breathing, urine formation, RAS, cAMP pathway, thyroid hormone synthesis, menstrual cycle, spermatogenesis, transcription and translation, micturition reflex, Ferguson reflex.
3. Quote standard values: RMP −70 mV, threshold −55 mV; CSF 150 mL (500 mL/day); TV 500 mL, VC 4600 mL, TLC 5800 mL; GFR 125 mL/min (180 L/day); urine 1–1.5 L/day; renal threshold for glucose 180 mg/dL; fasting glucose 70–100 mg/dL; plasma calcium 9–11 mg/dL; 46 chromosomes; menstrual cycle 28 days with ovulation about day 14.
4. Use comparison tables for "differentiate" questions: UMN vs LMN lesion, spermatogenesis vs oogenesis, DNA vs RNA, type 1 vs type 2 diabetes, Cushing's vs Addison's, cortical vs juxtamedullary nephron, obstructive vs restrictive lung disease, myxoedema vs Graves' disease.
5. End with a pharmacy link — the drug that acts on that step: PPIs on the proton pump, H2 blockers on histamine, local anaesthetics on Na+ channels, benzodiazepines on GABA, furosemide on the loop of Henle, ACE inhibitors on RAS, carbimazole on thyroid peroxidase, sulphonylureas on the β-cell K+ channel, oral contraceptives on the LH surge, antibiotics on bacterial ribosomes. Examiners in a pharmacy course reward this.
6. Learn the "lists of names" that MCQs love: Brodmann areas (4, 3-1-2, 17, 41-42, 44-45, 22), the four ventricles and their connecting foramina, three salivary ducts (Stensen's, Wharton's, Rivinus), gastric cell types, the three zones of the adrenal cortex, the four islet cell types, stop and start codons.
7. For disorders, write a two-column table (cause → key features) rather than long paragraphs; it is quicker to write and easier to mark.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five answers with full diagrams: **action potential with synaptic transmission**, **HCl secretion and phases of gastric secretion**, **physiology of urine formation with the nephron**, **thyroid hormone synthesis with hypo- and hyperthyroidism**, and **the menstrual cycle with spermatogenesis and oogenesis**. Then revise the tables below.

| 4 | Pituitary with hypothalamus and portal system; thyroid follicle; adrenal zones; cAMP pathway |
| 5 | Male and female reproductive organs; menstrual cycle chart; sperm; DNA double helix |

| Small intestine / large intestine | About 5–6 m / about 1.5 m |
| ATP energy per high-energy bond | About 7.3 kcal/mol |
| BMR | About 40 kcal/m²/h (men), 37 (women); +13% per °C of fever |

| PCO2 arterial / venous | 40 / 46 mmHg |
| O2 carried | 1.34 mL per g Hb; 97–98.5% as oxyhaemoglobin |
| CO2 carried | 70% bicarbonate, 23% carbamino, 7% dissolved |

| Renal blood flow | About 1200–1300 mL/min (20–25% of cardiac output) |
| GFR | 125 mL/min (180 L/day); NFP about 10 mmHg |

| Adrenal medulla | Adrenaline about 80%, noradrenaline about 20% |

| Spermatogenesis | About 64–74 days; 4 sperm per primary spermatocyte |

| Genetic code | 64 codons; start AUG; stop UAA, UAG, UGA |

**One-line facts**

- Myelin: oligodendrocytes in CNS, Schwann cells in PNS; saltatory conduction at nodes of Ranvier.
- Glutamate excites, GABA inhibits the brain; glycine inhibits the spinal cord.
- CSF flow: lateral ventricles → foramen of Monro → third ventricle → aqueduct → fourth ventricle → Luschka and Magendie → subarachnoid space → arachnoid villi.
- Medulla: cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centres; pyramids cross here.
- Cerebellar lesion: ataxia, intention tremor, past-pointing (same side).
- Pain and temperature: lateral spinothalamic (cross in cord); fine touch and position: dorsal column (cross in medulla).
- UMN lesion: spastic, brisk reflexes, Babinski positive; LMN lesion: flaccid, wasting, reflexes lost.
- Parietal cells: HCl + intrinsic factor; proton pump = H+/K+ ATPase; acid driven by ACh (M3), gastrin and histamine (H2).
- Pepsinogen → pepsin by HCl; trypsinogen → trypsin by enterokinase.
- B12 and bile salts absorbed in terminal ileum; iron and calcium in duodenum.
- Creatine phosphate + ADP ⇌ creatine + ATP (creatine kinase).
- Surfactant from type II cells; CO2 is the strongest stimulus to breathe.
- Bohr effect: CO2 and H+ release O2; Haldane effect: O2 releases CO2.
- ADH → aquaporin-2 (water); aldosterone → Na+ kept, K+ lost.
- RAS: renin (JG cells) → angiotensin I → ACE (lungs) → angiotensin II.
- Second messengers: cAMP, IP3/DAG/Ca2+; insulin uses tyrosine kinase; steroids act on genes.
- GH excess: gigantism (child), acromegaly (adult); ADH lack: diabetes insipidus.
- Carbimazole blocks thyroid peroxidase; iodine deficiency → goitre.
- Low PTH → tetany (Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs).
- Adrenal cortex: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens).
- Cushing's: moon face, buffalo hump; Addison's: hypotension, pigmentation.
- Melatonin rises in darkness; thymus matures T cells.
- Leydig cells → testosterone (LH); Sertoli cells → spermatogenesis (FSH), inhibin.
- Oestrogen → proliferative phase; progesterone → secretory phase; LH surge → ovulation.
- Fertilization in ampulla; cortical reaction blocks polyspermy; hCG keeps the corpus luteum.
- Ferguson reflex: cervical stretch → oxytocin → stronger contractions (positive feedback).
- Down syndrome trisomy 21; Turner 45 XO; Klinefelter 47 XXY.
- Haemophilia and colour blindness: X-linked recessive; sickle cell and thalassaemia: autosomal recessive.

# Study of the integumentary system and special senses using models and specimens

**Aim:** To study the structure of the skin and of the organs of special sense (eye, ear, nose and tongue) with the help of models, charts and specimens.

## Principle

Models and charts show in three dimensions what a textbook shows in one plane. By identifying each part on the model, drawing it and stating its function, the student links structure with function. The skin is the largest organ and part of the integumentary system; the eye, ear, nose and tongue carry receptors for sight, hearing and balance, smell and taste (theory in BP101T).

## Requirements

Models of a skin section, eyeball (dissectible), ear (external, middle and inner), nasal cavity and tongue; wall charts; preserved specimens if available (e.g. sheep or goat eye); pointer, drawing sheets, pencil.

## Procedure

1. Place each model on the table in its anatomical position.
2. Identify the parts listed below on the model, then on the chart.
3. For a dissectible model, separate the layers carefully and replace them in order.
4. Draw a neat labelled diagram of each organ in the record book and write two or three functions.
5. If a preserved eye is provided, examine it with gloves: cut it into front and back halves and identify the cornea, lens, vitreous body and retina.

## Observations

| Organ | Parts to identify | Functions to note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Skin (section)** | Epidermis (stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum in thick skin, corneum), dermis (papillary and reticular layers), hypodermis; hair follicle with arrector pili muscle, sebaceous gland, sweat gland and duct, Meissner's corpuscle, Pacinian corpuscle, blood vessels | Protection, temperature regulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis, excretion of sweat |
| **Eyeball** | Sclera, cornea, choroid, ciliary body, iris, pupil, lens with suspensory ligaments, aqueous humour, vitreous body, retina, macula lutea (fovea), optic disc (blind spot), optic nerve; extrinsic eye muscles | Focusing light on the retina; rods for dim light, cones for colour |
| **Ear** | External: auricle, external acoustic meatus, tympanic membrane. Middle: malleus, incus, stapes, Eustachian (auditory) tube. Inner: cochlea (organ of Corti), vestibule, three semicircular canals | Hearing; balance (vestibular apparatus) |
| **Nose** | External nose, nasal septum, conchae (turbinates), meatuses, olfactory epithelium in the roof, paranasal sinus openings | Filtering, warming and moistening air; smell |
| **Tongue** | Tip, body, root, sulcus terminalis; papillae — circumvallate (in a V in front of the sulcus), fungiform, filiform (no taste buds), foliate | Taste, chewing, swallowing, speech |

```text
 SKIN (vertical section)
  ________________________________  stratum corneum
 |  EPIDERMIS  (no blood vessels)  |  stratum basale
 |~~~~~~~~~~ dermal papillae ~~~~~~|  <- Meissner's corpuscle
 |  DERMIS: hair follicle, sebaceous|
 |  gland, sweat gland, vessels,    |
 |  arrector pili muscle            |
 |__________________________________|
 |  HYPODERMIS: fat, Pacinian corp. |
 |__________________________________|
```

## Result

The structure of the skin, eye, ear, nose and tongue was studied on models and charts, and labelled diagrams were drawn.

## Precautions

1. Handle dissectible models gently and reassemble them in the correct order.
2. Wear gloves for preserved specimens and wash hands afterwards.
3. Draw diagrams in pencil with straight label lines; do not copy colours.

## Viva questions

1. **Which layer of the epidermis divides to form new cells?** Stratum basale (germinativum).
2. **Which receptor in the skin senses deep pressure and vibration?** Pacinian corpuscle.
3. **What is the blind spot?** The optic disc, where the optic nerve leaves; it has no rods or cones.
4. **Name the smallest bone of the body.** Stapes, in the middle ear.
5. **Which part of the inner ear detects rotation of the head?** The semicircular canals.
6. **Which papillae of the tongue have no taste buds?** Filiform papillae.
7. **Why does a cold block the sense of smell?** Swollen mucosa and mucus stop odour molecules reaching the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nose.

# Study of the nervous system using models and specimens

**Aim:** To study the gross structure of the brain, spinal cord and nerves with the help of models, charts and specimens.

## Principle

The brain and spinal cord are best understood by identifying their parts on a model or preserved specimen and relating each part to its function (Unit 1). A dissectible brain model shows the lobes, the brainstem, the cerebellum and the ventricles; a spinal cord model shows the grey and white matter and the roots of the spinal nerves.

## Requirements

Dissectible model of the human brain (with midsagittal half), model of the brain ventricles, model or chart of the spinal cord in transverse section and with vertebral column, chart of cranial nerves, chart of the autonomic nervous system; preserved sheep or goat brain if available; gloves, pointer, drawing sheets.

## Procedure

1. Study the **lateral surface** of the brain model: identify lobes and sulci.
2. Separate the two halves and study the **midsagittal surface**.
3. Study the **inferior surface (base)**: brainstem and the origins of cranial nerves.
4. Use the ventricle model to trace the flow of CSF.
5. Study the spinal cord model and a cross-section chart.
6. Draw labelled diagrams and write the function of each part.

## Observations

| View / model | Parts to identify |
| --- | --- |
| Lateral surface | Frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes; central sulcus; lateral sulcus; precentral (motor) and postcentral (sensory) gyri; cerebellum; pons; medulla |
| Midsagittal section | Corpus callosum, lateral ventricle (septum pellucidum), thalamus, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, pineal gland, third ventricle, midbrain with cerebral aqueduct, pons, medulla, fourth ventricle, cerebellum (arbor vitae) |
| Inferior surface | Olfactory bulbs and tracts, optic chiasma, mammillary bodies, cerebral peduncles, pons, pyramids of the medulla, roots of cranial nerves III–XII |
| Ventricles | Two lateral ventricles, foramina of Monro, third ventricle, aqueduct, fourth ventricle |
| Spinal cord | Cervical and lumbar enlargements, conus medullaris, filum terminale, cauda equina; in section: dorsal, lateral and ventral horns, central canal, white columns, dorsal root with ganglion, ventral root, spinal nerve |
| Meninges (chart) | Dura mater, arachnoid mater, subarachnoid space, pia mater |

```text
 BRAIN - midsagittal section
        ___ corpus callosum ______________
       /    lateral ventricle             \
      |  thalamus | 3rd ventricle          |  cerebrum
      | hypothalamus                       |
       \ pituitary   midbrain -- aqueduct /
                     pons ---- 4th ventricle -- cerebellum
                     medulla
                       |
                   spinal cord
```

## Result

The parts of the brain, spinal cord and meninges were identified on models and charts, and their functions recorded.

## Precautions

1. Handle models gently; do not force parts apart.
2. Use gloves for preserved brain specimens (formalin is irritant) and work in a ventilated room.
3. Return each removable part to its correct place.

## Viva questions

1. **What connects the two cerebral hemispheres?** The corpus callosum.
2. **Which gyrus is the primary motor area?** The precentral gyrus (area 4).
3. **Where do the corticospinal fibres cross?** At the pyramids of the medulla.
4. **Where does the spinal cord end in adults?** At the lower border of L1 or upper L2.
5. **What is the arbor vitae?** The tree-like white matter of the cerebellum.
6. **Which part of the brain is the relay station for sensations?** The thalamus.
7. **In which space is CSF found?** The subarachnoid space.

# Study of the endocrine system using models and specimens

**Aim:** To study the location, shape and parts of the endocrine glands with the help of models, charts and specimens.

## Principle

Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood (Unit 4). Each gland has a fixed position in the body and a typical shape that can be recognised on a torso model and on charts. Knowing their location explains clinical facts such as the visual field loss of pituitary tumours or the risk to the parathyroids during thyroid surgery.

## Requirements

Human torso model, models of the brain (for pituitary and pineal), thyroid with larynx and trachea, kidney with adrenal gland, pancreas with duodenum; charts of the endocrine system and of the hypothalamic–pituitary axis; pointer, drawing sheets.

## Procedure

1. On the torso model, locate each endocrine gland and note its relation to nearby organs.
2. Study each gland model separately and identify its parts.
3. Draw a chart showing the gland, its hormones and their main actions.
4. Draw labelled diagrams of the pituitary, thyroid and adrenal gland.

## Observations

| Gland | Location and relations | Parts | Hormones |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pituitary | In the sella turcica of the sphenoid, below the hypothalamus; optic chiasma above | Anterior lobe, posterior lobe, stalk (infundibulum) | GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin; ADH and oxytocin (posterior) |
| Pineal | Epithalamus, behind the third ventricle | — | Melatonin |
| Thyroid | Front of the neck, below the larynx, around the trachea | Two lobes, isthmus (2nd–4th tracheal rings) | T3, T4, calcitonin |
| Parathyroids | Back of the thyroid lobes (usually 4) | — | PTH |
| Thymus | Upper anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum | Two lobes | Thymosin |
| Adrenals | On top of each kidney (right pyramidal, left crescentic) | Cortex (three zones), medulla | Aldosterone, cortisol, androgens; adrenaline, noradrenaline |
| Pancreas | Behind the stomach; head in the C of the duodenum, tail at the spleen | Head, neck, body, tail; islets scattered inside | Insulin, glucagon, somatostatin |
| Gonads | Testes in scrotum; ovaries beside the uterus | — | Testosterone; oestrogen, progesterone |

```text
 Hypothalamus
     |  stalk
 [ANTERIOR | POSTERIOR]  pituitary
     |            \
 TSH ACTH GH       ADH, oxytocin
 FSH LH PRL
  |    |
 thyroid adrenal cortex, gonads, breast ...
```

## Result

The endocrine glands were located on the torso model, their parts identified and the hormones they secrete recorded.

## Precautions

1. Keep the torso model upright and replace removable organs correctly.
2. Note relations as well as position — they are commonly asked in viva.

## Viva questions

1. **Which gland is called the master gland?** The anterior pituitary, because it controls several other glands (though it is itself controlled by the hypothalamus).
2. **Why can a pituitary tumour affect vision?** It presses on the optic chiasma above it.
3. **Where are the parathyroid glands?** On the back of the thyroid lobes, usually two on each side.
4. **Name the three zones of the adrenal cortex.** Glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis.
5. **Which gland shrinks after puberty?** The thymus.
6. **Which part of the pancreas lies in the curve of the duodenum?** The head.

# Demonstration of the general neurological examination

**Aim:** To demonstrate the steps of a general neurological examination of a healthy subject: higher functions, cranial nerves, motor system, sensory system, reflexes and coordination.

## Principle

A neurological examination tests each part of the nervous system in turn. Because each function depends on a known pathway (Unit 1), an abnormal finding tells where the lesion is — for example, weakness with brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response points to an upper motor neuron lesion. In the laboratory the examination is demonstrated on a healthy classmate.

## Requirements

Knee hammer (reflex hammer), cotton wisp, pin with a blunt end (or neuro-tip), tuning fork (128 Hz), test tubes of warm and cold water, torch, Snellen chart, small familiar objects (coin, key), smelling bottles, couch.

## Procedure

**A. Higher functions**

1. **Consciousness:** note whether the subject is alert; in patients the Glasgow Coma Scale is used (eye 4 + verbal 5 + motor 6 = 15, fully conscious).
2. **Orientation:** to time, place and person.
3. **Memory:** recall three words after 5 minutes; recent and remote events.
4. **Speech:** fluency, understanding, naming objects.

**B. Cranial nerves (brief screen)**

| Nerve | Test |
| --- | --- |
| I Olfactory | Identify familiar smells, each nostril separately |
| II Optic | Visual acuity (Snellen), fields by confrontation, pupillary light reflex |
| III, IV, VI | Eye movements in all directions (follow a finger in an "H"); pupil size |
| V Trigeminal | Facial touch sensation; clench teeth (masseter); corneal reflex (demonstrated only, not done routinely) |
| VII Facial | Raise eyebrows, close eyes tightly, show teeth, puff cheeks |
| VIII Vestibulocochlear | Whispered voice; Rinne and Weber tuning-fork tests |
| IX, X | Say "aah" — palate rises in the midline; swallowing |
| XI Accessory | Shrug shoulders and turn head against resistance |
| XII Hypoglossal | Protrude tongue — it stays in the midline |

**C. Motor system**

1. **Bulk:** look for wasting; compare both sides.
2. **Tone:** passively move the limbs at elbow and knee; feel for stiffness or floppiness.
3. **Power:** test major muscle groups against resistance; grade on the MRC scale.
4. **Involuntary movements:** tremor, twitching.

**D. Sensory system** (eyes closed; compare both sides)

1. Light touch with cotton; pain with the blunt pin.
2. Temperature with warm and cold tubes.
3. Vibration with the tuning fork on bony points.
4. Position sense: move a finger or toe up or down; subject reports direction.
5. Stereognosis: identify a coin or key placed in the hand.

**E. Reflexes** — superficial (plantar, abdominal) and deep tendon (biceps, triceps, supinator, knee, ankle); see the reflex activity practical.

**F. Coordination and gait**

1. **Finger–nose test** and **heel–shin test**.
2. **Rapid alternating movements** (pronation–supination).
3. **Romberg's test:** stand with feet together, first with eyes open, then closed.
4. **Gait:** walk normally and heel-to-toe (tandem).

## Observations

| Test | Normal finding | Subject's finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consciousness, orientation | Alert, oriented (GCS 15) | |
| Cranial nerves I–XII | Intact | |
| Tone, power | Normal tone; power 5/5 in all limbs | |
| Sensations | Touch, pain, temperature, vibration and position sense normal and equal | |
| Reflexes | Present and equal (2+); plantar flexor | |
| Coordination | Finger–nose and heel–shin accurate; Romberg negative | |
| Gait | Normal, steady | |

**MRC power scale:** 0 no contraction; 1 flicker; 2 movement with gravity eliminated; 3 movement against gravity; 4 against some resistance; 5 normal power.

## Result

A general neurological examination was demonstrated on the subject; higher functions, cranial nerves, motor and sensory systems, reflexes and coordination were found ______ (normal / note any abnormality).

## Precautions

1. Explain each step and get consent; keep the subject relaxed and warm.
2. Always compare right and left sides.
3. Use only a blunt pin; never break the skin. Do not touch the cornea in routine class demonstrations.
4. Stand close to the subject during Romberg's test to prevent a fall.

## Viva questions

1. **What does a positive Romberg's test indicate?** Loss of position sense (dorsal column or sensory nerve disease): the subject sways or falls with eyes closed.
2. **What is the normal plantar response in adults?** Flexor (toes curl down); an extensor response (Babinski sign) indicates an UMN lesion.
3. **Which nerve is tested by asking the subject to protrude the tongue?** The hypoglossal nerve (XII).
4. **What is the maximum Glasgow Coma Scale score?** 15.
5. **Which tract carries vibration and position sense?** The dorsal column (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus).
6. **What does past-pointing in the finger–nose test suggest?** A cerebellar lesion on the same side.

# Demonstration of the function of the olfactory nerve

**Aim:** To test the sense of smell and so the function of the olfactory nerve (cranial nerve I) on each side.

## Principle

Odour molecules dissolve in the mucus of the **olfactory epithelium** in the roof of the nasal cavity and stimulate the bipolar olfactory receptor cells. Their axons pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid as the olfactory nerve to the olfactory bulb, then by the olfactory tract to the olfactory cortex in the temporal lobe. Each nostril is tested separately because a one-sided loss can point to a local lesion. Pungent substances such as ammonia are **not** used: they stimulate pain fibres of the trigeminal nerve and give a false "smell" even when the olfactory nerve is damaged.

## Requirements

A set of labelled-underneath smelling bottles with familiar, non-irritant odours (coffee powder, clove oil, peppermint, camphor, rose water, soap, lemon), cotton wool, a blindfold, water for rinsing.

## Procedure

1. Check that both nostrils are clear (ask the subject to breathe through each in turn). Make sure the subject has no cold.
2. Blindfold the subject or ask them to close their eyes.
3. Close the left nostril by pressing it gently. Hold an open bottle about 2–3 cm below the right nostril.
4. Ask the subject to sniff and say whether a smell is present, then name it.
5. Repeat with three or four different odours, in random order, with a gap of 30–60 seconds between them to avoid adaptation.
6. Repeat the test for the left nostril.
7. **Adaptation:** hold one odour under the nostril continuously and note the time after which the subject no longer notices it.

## Observations

| Odour | Right nostril: perceived / identified | Left nostril: perceived / identified |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coffee | | |
| Clove oil | | |
| Peppermint | | |
| Soap | | |

Time to adaptation for continuous exposure: ______ seconds.

**Interpretation:** normal (**normosmia**) — each odour is perceived and named on both sides; **hyposmia** — reduced; **anosmia** — absent; **parosmia** — distorted smell.

## Result

The sense of smell was ______ on the right side and ______ on the left side; the olfactory nerve function is ______.

## Precautions

1. Test one nostril at a time and close the other without pressing on the septum.
2. Use familiar, non-irritant substances only.
3. Do not let the subject see the bottle.
4. Allow time between odours and close each bottle after use.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is ammonia not used to test smell?** It stimulates trigeminal pain endings and can be "felt" even if the olfactory nerve is cut.
2. **Through which bone do olfactory nerve fibres pass?** The cribriform plate of the ethmoid.
3. **What is anosmia?** Complete loss of smell.
4. **Name common causes of anosmia.** Common cold and sinusitis, head injury fracturing the cribriform plate, viral infection, ageing, Parkinson's disease.
5. **What is olfactory adaptation?** Fading of a smell sensation during continued exposure to the same odour.
6. **Is smell relayed through the thalamus before reaching the cortex?** No; smell is the only sensation that reaches the cortex without first relaying in the thalamus.
practicals.title: Demonstration of the function of the olfactory nerve

# Examination of the different types of taste

**Aim:** To examine the primary tastes — sweet, salty, sour and bitter (and umami) — on different areas of the tongue.

## Principle

Taste buds on the fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae contain receptor cells that respond to chemicals dissolved in saliva. Sweet, bitter and umami act on G-protein receptors; salty (Na+) and sour (H+) act through ion channels. Impulses travel in the **facial nerve (VII, chorda tympani)** from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and the **glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)** from the posterior third, to the medulla, thalamus and the gustatory cortex. The old "tongue map" with one taste per zone is not correct: all tastes can be sensed over all areas with taste buds, though the threshold differs a little between regions — which this practical shows.

## Requirements

Dilute solutions in labelled dropper bottles, as prepared by the laboratory: sweet — sucrose; salty — sodium chloride; sour — citric acid or vinegar; bitter — a very dilute quinine solution or another approved bitter; optionally umami — monosodium glutamate. Cotton-tipped applicators, a glass of water, paper napkins, a tongue diagram.

## Procedure

1. Ask the subject to rinse the mouth with water and keep the tongue protruded throughout (so the solution does not spread).
2. Dry the tongue gently with a napkin.
3. Dip a fresh applicator in the sweet solution and touch it on the tip of the tongue. Ask the subject to point to the written word (sweet, salty, sour, bitter, none) without speaking.
4. Repeat on the sides (front and back) and the back of the tongue, rinsing between tests.
5. Repeat with salty, sour and finally bitter solutions (bitter last because its taste lingers).
6. Test each side of the tongue separately to compare right and left.
7. Mark the results on a tongue diagram.

## Observations

| Solution | Tip | Front sides | Back sides | Back (posterior third) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sweet | | | | |
| Salty | | | | |
| Sour | | | | |
| Bitter | | | | |

Use + (tasted), ++ (strong) and − (not tasted). Typically sweet is quickly noticed at the tip, sour on the sides and bitter at the back, but each taste is detected in several areas.

**Terms:** **ageusia** — loss of taste; **hypogeusia** — reduced taste; **dysgeusia** — distorted taste (e.g. metallic taste with metronidazole).

## Result

All primary tastes were perceived on the tongue of the subject, with the following areas of greater sensitivity: ______.

## Precautions

1. Use fresh, clean applicators for each solution and each area.
2. Keep the tongue protruded and rinse between tests.
3. Use only very dilute, safe solutions; do not let the subject swallow them.
4. Test bitter last.

## Viva questions

1. **Which nerves carry taste?** Facial (VII) from the anterior two-thirds, glossopharyngeal (IX) from the posterior third, vagus (X) from the epiglottis region.
2. **Which papillae carry the most taste buds?** Circumvallate papillae.
3. **Why must a substance be dissolved to be tasted?** Taste receptors respond only to chemicals in solution.
4. **What is umami?** The savoury taste of glutamate.
5. **Why does food taste bland during a cold?** Much of flavour depends on smell, which is reduced.
6. **Name a drug that alters taste.** Metronidazole (metallic taste); also captopril, lithium.
practicals.title: Examination of the different types of taste

# Demonstration of visual acuity

**Aim:** To determine the distant and near visual acuity of the subject using the Snellen chart and a near-vision chart.

## Principle

**Visual acuity** is the ability of the eye to see fine detail — to distinguish two points as separate. It depends on a clear cornea and lens, correct focusing and the dense packing of cones at the **fovea**. A normal eye can separate two points that subtend an angle of **1 minute of arc** at the eye. Each letter of the **Snellen chart** is drawn so that it subtends 5 minutes of arc as a whole (each stroke 1 minute) at the distance marked beside its row.

Acuity is written as a fraction: **V = d / D**, where d = distance of the subject from the chart (6 m in India) and D = distance at which a normal eye can read that row. Normal distant acuity is **6/6**.

## Requirements

Snellen's test-type chart (rows marked 60, 36, 24, 18, 12, 9, 6, 5 m), a well-lit room at least 6 m long (or a mirror arrangement for 3 m), an occluder or card, a near-vision chart (Jaeger or N-notation), pinhole disc, measuring tape.

## Procedure

**A. Distant vision**

1. Hang the Snellen chart at eye level in good, even light. Seat the subject exactly **6 m** away.
2. Cover the left eye with the occluder (without pressing on it).
3. Ask the subject to read the letters from the top row downwards with the right eye.
4. Note the smallest row read correctly (allowing at most one error). Record as 6/D.
5. Repeat for the left eye, then both eyes together.
6. If the subject cannot read 6/6, repeat looking through a **pinhole**; improvement means a refractive error that glasses can correct.
7. If the top letter (60) cannot be read at 6 m, move the subject closer (5, 4, 3 m...) and record as, e.g., 3/60. If still not read, test finger counting, hand movements and perception of light.

**B. Near vision**

1. Hold the near-vision chart about 33–35 cm from the eye in good light.
2. Test each eye separately; record the smallest print read (e.g. N6 or J1).

## Observations

| Eye | Distant vision | With pinhole | Near vision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Right | 6/ | 6/ | N |
| Left | 6/ | 6/ | N |
| Both | 6/ | — | N |

**Interpretation**

| Finding | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 6/6 | Normal distant acuity |
| 6/5 | Better than average |
| 6/9 to 6/60 | Reduced acuity; improves with pinhole if refractive error |
| Distant poor, near good | Myopia (corrected with concave lens) |
| Near poor (especially after 40 years) | Hypermetropia or presbyopia (convex lens) |

## Result

Visual acuity of the right eye is ______, of the left eye ______ (distant); near vision ______.

## Precautions

1. Keep exactly 6 m distance and good, uniform illumination.
2. Test each eye separately; cover the other eye without pressing on it.
3. The subject should not squint, lean forward or memorise the chart.
4. If the subject wears glasses for distance, record acuity with and without them.

## Viva questions

1. **What is normal visual acuity?** 6/6 (20/20 in feet).
2. **What does 6/60 mean?** The subject reads at 6 m what a normal eye reads at 60 m.
3. **Which part of the retina gives the sharpest vision?** The fovea centralis, which has only cones.
4. **Why does a pinhole improve vision in refractive errors?** It lets through only central rays that need little focusing, reducing blur.
5. **Which lens corrects myopia?** A concave (diverging) lens.
6. **What is presbyopia?** Loss of near focusing with age as the lens becomes less elastic.
practicals.title: Demonstration of visual acuity

practicals.markdown:
# Demonstration of reflex activity

**Aim:** To elicit and record the common superficial and deep (tendon) reflexes in a human subject.

## Principle

A reflex is an automatic response to a stimulus through a **reflex arc** — receptor, afferent neuron, centre in the spinal cord or brainstem, efferent neuron and effector (Unit 1). **Deep tendon (stretch) reflexes** are monosynaptic: a sharp tap on a tendon stretches the muscle spindles, which excite the α motor neurons of the same muscle, so it contracts. **Superficial reflexes** are polysynaptic responses to stroking the skin or mucosa. Each reflex tests a known spinal segment; exaggerated reflexes suggest an upper motor neuron lesion and absent reflexes a lower motor neuron or sensory lesion.

## Requirements

Knee hammer, cotton wisp, blunt key or the handle of the hammer for the plantar reflex, torch, couch.

## Procedure

1. Explain the test and make the subject sit or lie relaxed; the limb tested should be slightly stretched and loose.
2. Hold the hammer loosely and let it fall with a brisk wrist movement on the tendon.
3. Compare each reflex on both sides.
4. If a reflex is absent, use **reinforcement**: for leg reflexes ask the subject to clench the teeth or hook the fingers and pull (Jendrassik's manoeuvre) at the moment of the tap.

**Deep tendon reflexes**

| Reflex | Method | Response | Segment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Biceps jerk** | Elbow half-bent, examiner's thumb on biceps tendon; tap the thumb | Biceps contracts, elbow flexes | C5–C6 |
| **Supinator (brachioradialis) jerk** | Forearm half-pronated on the lap; tap the lower end of the radius | Elbow flexes | C5–C6 |
| **Triceps jerk** | Arm supported, elbow bent at 90°; tap triceps tendon above the olecranon | Elbow extends | C6–C7 |
| **Knee jerk (patellar)** | Sitting with legs hanging freely (or knees supported when lying); tap patellar tendon below the patella | Quadriceps contracts, leg extends | L2–L4 (mainly L3–L4) |
| **Ankle jerk** | Foot slightly dorsiflexed; tap the Achilles tendon | Plantar flexion of the foot | S1–S2 |

**Superficial reflexes**

| Reflex | Method | Normal response | Segment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Plantar reflex** | Stroke the outer edge of the sole from heel to the little toe, then across to the big toe, with a blunt object | Flexion of toes (flexor plantar) | L5–S1 (S1–S2) |
| Abdominal reflex | Stroke the abdominal skin from outside towards the umbilicus in each quadrant | Umbilicus moves towards the side stroked | T7–T12 |
| Corneal reflex | (Demonstrated only) light touch of the cornea with a cotton wisp from the side | Blinking of both eyes | V (afferent), VII (efferent) |
| Pupillary light reflex | Shine a torch into one eye | Constriction of both pupils (direct and consensual) | II (afferent), III (efferent) |

## Observations

| Reflex | Right | Left |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Biceps | | |
| Triceps | | |
| Supinator | | |
| Knee | | |
| Ankle | | |
| Plantar | | |
| Pupillary | | |

**Grading of tendon reflexes:** 0 absent; 1+ diminished; 2+ normal; 3+ brisk (more than normal); 4+ very brisk with clonus.

**Babinski sign:** dorsiflexion of the big toe with fanning of the other toes on plantar stimulation — normal in infants under about one year, abnormal (UMN lesion) in adults.

## Result

The deep and superficial reflexes of the subject were elicited and found to be ______ (present and equal / note abnormalities); plantar response ______.

## Precautions

1. The subject must be relaxed; tension can abolish a reflex.
2. Strike the tendon, not the muscle belly, with a brisk, light tap.
3. Always compare both sides with equal force.
4. Use reinforcement before calling a reflex absent.
5. Do not use a sharp object for the plantar reflex.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the knee jerk called monosynaptic?** The Ia afferent fibre from the muscle spindle synapses directly on the α motor neuron.
2. **What is the receptor for a stretch reflex?** The muscle spindle.
3. **What does an exaggerated knee jerk indicate?** An upper motor neuron lesion (loss of descending inhibition), anxiety or hyperthyroidism.
4. **What is Jendrassik's manoeuvre?** Reinforcement by pulling hooked fingers apart, which increases the excitability of spinal motor neurons.
5. **Name the segment tested by the ankle jerk.** S1–S2.
6. **What is a consensual light reflex?** Constriction of the opposite pupil when light is shone into one eye.
practicals.title: Demonstration of reflex activity

practicals.markdown:
# Recording of body temperature

**Aim:** To record the oral and axillary body temperature of the subject using a clinical thermometer, and to note the effect of exercise.

## Principle

Body temperature is held near **37 °C** by the heat-regulating centre in the **hypothalamus**, which balances heat production (metabolism, muscle activity) and heat loss (radiation, conduction, convection, evaporation of sweat) by negative feedback. Temperature varies with the site of measurement: rectal (core) is about 0.5 °C higher and axillary about 0.5 °C lower than oral. It also shows a daily rhythm (lowest early morning, highest late afternoon), rises slightly after ovulation and with exercise, and rises in fever when the hypothalamic set point is raised.

## Requirements

Digital clinical thermometer (or a clinical glass thermometer, 35–42 °C, with a constriction that holds the reading), spirit swabs, cotton, watch, record sheet. (Mercury thermometers are being replaced by digital ones because mercury is toxic if the glass breaks.)

## Procedure

**A. Oral temperature**

1. The subject should not have eaten, drunk, smoked or exercised for 15–30 minutes.
2. Clean the thermometer with a spirit swab and let it dry. For a glass thermometer, shake the column down below 35 °C.
3. Place the bulb **under the tongue** to one side of the frenulum; ask the subject to close the lips (not the teeth) and breathe through the nose.
4. Leave it for the time given by the maker (digital: until it beeps; glass: about 2–3 minutes).
5. Remove, read at eye level and record. Clean the thermometer again.

**B. Axillary temperature**

1. Dry the armpit with a towel.
2. Place the bulb in the centre of the axilla and hold the arm against the chest.
3. Leave it longer (glass: about 5 minutes; digital: until it beeps). Read and record.

**C. Effect of exercise**

1. Ask the subject to do moderate exercise (e.g. spot running for 3–5 minutes).
2. Record the oral temperature again immediately and after 10 minutes of rest.

## Observations

| Site / condition | Temperature (°C) | Temperature (°F) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oral, at rest | | |
| Axillary, at rest | | |
| Oral, after exercise | | |
| Oral, 10 min after rest | | |

**Conversion:** °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32. **Worked example:** 37 °C = (37 × 1.8) + 32 = **98.6 °F**.

**Normal values (approximate):** oral 36.5–37.2 °C (97.7–99 °F); axillary about 0.5 °C lower than oral; rectal about 0.5 °C higher. Fever (pyrexia) is generally taken as an oral temperature above about 37.5 °C; hyperpyrexia above about 41 °C; hypothermia below 35 °C.

## Result

The oral temperature of the subject at rest was ______ °C and the axillary temperature ______ °C; after exercise the oral temperature rose to ______ °C.

## Precautions

1. Disinfect the thermometer before and after use.
2. Avoid hot or cold drinks, smoking and exercise before taking oral temperature.
3. Do not use the oral route in unconscious patients, small children or after mouth surgery.
4. Keep the thermometer in place for the full time.
5. Handle glass thermometers carefully; if one breaks, report it and do not touch the mercury.

## Viva questions

1. **Where is the temperature-regulating centre?** In the hypothalamus.
2. **What is the normal oral temperature?** About 37 °C (98.6 °F).
3. **Why is axillary temperature lower than oral?** The axilla is a skin site, partly exposed to the air, not a closed cavity near core blood.
4. **What is the purpose of the constriction in a clinical glass thermometer?** It stops the mercury falling back, so the maximum reading is held.
5. **How do antipyretics such as paracetamol reduce fever?** They inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in the hypothalamus and reset the raised set point.
6. **Name the ways the body loses heat.** Radiation, conduction, convection and evaporation of sweat.
practicals.title: Recording of body temperature

practicals.markdown:
# Demonstration of positive and negative feedback mechanisms

**Aim:** To demonstrate negative feedback control of blood pressure and heart rate on changing posture, and to explain positive feedback with examples.

## Principle

**Homeostasis** keeps the internal environment steady through feedback loops of receptor → control centre → effector.

- In **negative feedback** the response opposes the original change, restoring the set point. Example: on standing up, blood pools in the legs and BP falls; **baroreceptors** in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire less; the cardiovascular centres in the medulla increase sympathetic activity, so heart rate and vessel tone rise and BP returns to normal within seconds (baroreceptor reflex). Other examples: blood glucose and insulin, body temperature, thyroid hormone (TRH–TSH–T4).
- In **positive feedback** the response increases the original change until an outside event stops it. Examples: oxytocin and uterine contractions in labour (Ferguson reflex), the LH surge before ovulation, blood clotting, and the opening of Na+ channels in an action potential.

## Requirements

Sphygmomanometer and stethoscope (or a digital BP monitor), stopwatch, couch; charts of feedback loops (labour, clotting, LH surge).

## Procedure

**A. Negative feedback — posture and the baroreceptor reflex**

1. Let the subject lie on the couch for 5 minutes.
2. Record pulse rate and BP in the lying position.
3. Ask the subject to stand up quickly. Record pulse and BP **immediately**, then at 1, 2 and 3 minutes.
4. Note the immediate change and the return towards the resting values.

**B. Positive feedback — study from charts**

1. Draw the loop of the Ferguson reflex: baby's head stretches the cervix → oxytocin from posterior pituitary → stronger contractions → more stretch → more oxytocin, ending with delivery.
2. Draw the loops for blood clotting (thrombin activates more clotting factors) and the LH surge.

## Observations

| Position / time | Pulse (/min) | Systolic BP (mmHg) | Diastolic BP (mmHg) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lying (rest) | | | |
| Standing — immediately | | | |
| Standing — 1 min | | | |
| Standing — 2 min | | | |
| Standing — 3 min | | | |

**Expected:** on standing, the systolic BP may fall slightly for a moment and the pulse rises by about 10–20 beats/min; within 1–2 minutes BP is restored (diastolic often slightly higher than lying) — the change is corrected, showing **negative feedback**. A fall of systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more that persists, with dizziness, is **orthostatic (postural) hypotension**, seen with some antihypertensive drugs (α-blockers), dehydration and autonomic neuropathy.

```text
 NEGATIVE FEEDBACK                         POSITIVE FEEDBACK
 BP falls (standing)                       cervix stretched
      |                                          |
 baroreceptors fire less                   oxytocin released
      |                                          |
 medulla: sympathetic UP, vagus DOWN       stronger contractions
      |                                          |
 heart rate UP, vessels constrict          more cervical stretch ---+
      |                                          ^                  |
 BP rises back to normal  (change REVERSED)      +------------------+
                                           (change AMPLIFIED until birth)
```

## Result

On changing posture from lying to standing, the heart rate rose by ______ /min and the BP returned to ______ mmHg within ______ minutes, demonstrating negative feedback. Positive feedback was explained with the examples of labour, clotting and the LH surge.

## Precautions

1. Stand close to the subject when they stand up, in case of dizziness.
2. Keep the cuff on and the arm at heart level for all readings.
3. Record readings quickly and at fixed times.
4. Do not do this test on anyone with a history of fainting without supervision.

## Viva questions

1. **Define homeostasis.** Maintenance of a relatively constant internal environment despite outside changes.
2. **Which type of feedback is more common in the body?** Negative feedback.
3. **Where are baroreceptors located?** In the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
4. **Give two examples of positive feedback.** Oxytocin in labour; blood clotting (also the LH surge).
5. **Why is positive feedback not used for routine control?** It amplifies change and would drive a value further from normal; it is used only for events that must be completed quickly.
6. **What is orthostatic hypotension?** A sustained fall in BP on standing, causing dizziness.
practicals.title: Demonstration of positive and negative feedback mechanisms

# Determination of tidal volume and vital capacity

**Aim:** To determine the tidal volume and vital capacity of the subject using a spirometer, and to calculate minute ventilation.

## Principle

A **spirometer** measures the volume of air breathed in and out. In the common water-sealed (Student's or Benedict–Roth type) spirometer, a light inverted drum floats in water; air breathed into it lifts the drum and air drawn out lowers it, and the movement is read on a scale (or recorded on a drum). Digital spirometers measure air flow electronically and calculate the volumes.

- **Tidal volume (TV):** air breathed in or out in one quiet breath — about 500 mL.
- **Vital capacity (VC):** maximum air breathed out after a maximum inspiration = IRV + TV + ERV — about 4.5–5 L in young adult men and about 3–3.5 L in women.
- **Minute ventilation = TV × respiratory rate.**

## Requirements

Spirometer (water-sealed or digital), disposable mouthpieces, nose clip, spirit swabs, stopwatch, measuring tape and weighing scale (to compare with predicted values).

## Procedure

1. Note the subject's age, sex, height and weight. Explain the procedure; the subject sits or stands upright.
2. Fix a clean disposable mouthpiece and put on the nose clip.
3. **Tidal volume:** ask the subject to breathe quietly through the mouthpiece for a few breaths to get used to it, then record the volume of 5–10 quiet breaths. Divide the total by the number of breaths.
4. Count the respiratory rate for one minute (without the subject being aware, if possible).
5. **Vital capacity:** ask the subject to take the deepest possible breath, place the lips tightly around the mouthpiece and breathe out as completely as possible, steadily. Read the volume.
6. Repeat the VC three times with a rest of a minute between attempts; take the highest value.
7. Optionally measure inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes.

## Observations and calculations

| Trial | Tidal volume (mL) | Vital capacity (mL) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | |
| 2 | | |
| 3 | | |
| Result | Mean | Highest |

Respiratory rate = ______ /min.

**Minute ventilation = TV × rate.** **Worked example:** TV 500 mL × 12/min = **6000 mL/min (6 L/min)**.

**Alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate** = (500 − 150) × 12 = 4200 mL/min.

**Factors that alter VC:** higher in tall people, men and athletes (swimmers); lower in women, the elderly, in the lying position, obesity, pregnancy, lung fibrosis, pleural effusion, weak respiratory muscles and asthma.

## Result

Tidal volume of the subject = ______ mL; vital capacity = ______ mL; minute ventilation = ______ L/min.

## Precautions

1. Use a new disposable mouthpiece for each subject and disinfect the equipment.
2. Make sure there is no leak around the lips or through the nose.
3. Expiration for VC should be complete and steady, after a truly maximal inspiration.
4. Allow rest between trials; stop if the subject feels dizzy.
5. Read the scale at eye level.

## Viva questions

1. **Define vital capacity.** The maximum volume of air that can be expelled after a maximum inspiration.
2. **Which volume cannot be measured with a simple spirometer?** Residual volume (and so FRC and TLC).
3. **What is the normal tidal volume?** About 500 mL.
4. **Why is VC lower when lying down?** Abdominal organs push the diaphragm up and blood volume in the lungs increases.
5. **What is dead space?** Air in the conducting airways that does not take part in gas exchange (about 150 mL).
6. **What is FEV1?** The volume expired in the first second of a forced expiration; normally about 80% of FVC, reduced in asthma and COPD.

# Study of the digestive, respiratory, cardiovascular, urinary and reproductive systems with models, charts and specimens

**Aim:** To identify the organs and the important parts of the digestive, respiratory, cardiovascular, urinary and reproductive systems on models, charts and specimens.

## Principle

Each system is first located on a human torso model, then studied in detail on separate organ models and charts. Knowing the position of organs and the parts of each one is the base for understanding their functions (Units 2, 3 and 5 of this subject, and the heart from BP101T) and is a common spotting and viva exercise.

## Requirements

Human torso model with removable organs; models of the stomach, liver, pancreas with duodenum, larynx and lungs, heart (dissectible), kidney (section) and nephron, male and female pelvis (sagittal section); wall charts; preserved specimens if available (e.g. sheep heart, kidney); gloves, pointer, drawing sheets.

## Procedure

1. On the torso model, identify each organ and note its position (abdominal regions, thoracic cavity, pelvis).
2. Remove organs in order (lungs, heart, stomach, intestines) and replace them in reverse order.
3. Study each organ model and identify the parts listed below.
4. For preserved specimens (with gloves), identify chambers, valves or regions as listed.
5. Draw labelled diagrams of the stomach, nephron, heart, lungs and male and female reproductive organs.

## Observations

| System | Organ / model | Parts to identify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Digestive | Torso and charts | Mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum and appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal |
| | Stomach | Cardia, fundus, body, pyloric antrum, pyloric sphincter, lesser and greater curvatures, rugae |
| | Liver, gallbladder, pancreas | Right and left lobes, falciform ligament, porta hepatis, gallbladder, cystic and common bile ducts; head, body and tail of pancreas, ampulla of Vater |
| Respiratory | Larynx and lungs | Thyroid and cricoid cartilages, epiglottis, trachea with C-shaped rings, carina, main bronchi; right lung 3 lobes (oblique and horizontal fissures), left lung 2 lobes with cardiac notch, hilum, pleura, diaphragm |
| Cardiovascular | Heart | Four chambers, interatrial and interventricular septa, tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic valves, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, aorta, pulmonary trunk, venae cavae, pulmonary veins, coronary arteries |
| Urinary | Kidney section, nephron, torso | Capsule, cortex, medulla, pyramids, papillae, calyces, pelvis, ureter; glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct; bladder (trigone), urethra |
| Reproductive (male) | Male pelvis | Testis, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, prostate, bulbourethral gland, urethra, penis |
| Reproductive (female) | Female pelvis | Ovary, uterine tube (fimbriae, ampulla, isthmus), uterus (fundus, body, cervix), vagina, relation to bladder (front) and rectum (behind) |

## Result

The organs and their parts of the digestive, respiratory, cardiovascular, urinary and reproductive systems were identified on models, charts and specimens, and labelled diagrams were drawn.

## Precautions

1. Remove and replace torso organs in the correct order without forcing them.
2. Wear gloves for preserved specimens and avoid inhaling formalin fumes.
3. Label diagrams neatly with straight lines.

## Viva questions

1. **Which lung has three lobes?** The right lung.
2. **Which part of the small intestine is the longest?** The ileum.
3. **Where does the common bile duct open?** Into the second part of the duodenum at the ampulla of Vater, with the main pancreatic duct.
4. **What is the trigone of the bladder?** A smooth triangular area between the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening.
5. **Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle?** The mitral (bicuspid) valve.
6. **Where does fertilization usually occur?** In the ampulla of the uterine tube.
7. **Which kidney lies lower and why?** The right kidney, because the liver lies above it.
practicals.title: Study of digestive, respiratory, cardiovascular, urinary and reproductive systems with models

# Recording of body mass index (BMI)

**Aim:** To measure the height and weight of the subject and calculate the body mass index.

The PCI practical list writes "basal mass index"; the standard measurement is the **body mass index (BMI)**, described here.

## Principle

**BMI** (Quetelet index) relates weight to height and is a simple screening measure of underweight, overweight and obesity in adults:

**BMI = weight (kg) ÷ [height (m)]²**, expressed in kg/m².

It does not measure body fat directly and cannot separate muscle from fat, so very muscular people may show a high BMI. Asians, including Indians, have more body fat and higher risk of diabetes and heart disease at a given BMI, so lower cut-offs are recommended for Indian adults.

## Requirements

Calibrated weighing scale (digital or beam), stadiometer or a measuring scale fixed to a wall with a head board, record sheet, calculator. Optionally a non-stretchable tape for waist circumference.

## Procedure

1. **Weight:** check that the scale reads zero. Ask the subject to remove shoes and heavy items and stand still in the centre of the platform. Read to the nearest 0.1 kg.
2. **Height:** subject stands barefoot, heels together, back, buttocks and heels touching the wall or stadiometer, looking straight ahead. Lower the head board to touch the top of the head. Read to the nearest 0.1 cm and convert to metres.
3. Calculate BMI with the formula.
4. Optionally measure **waist circumference** midway between the lowest rib and the iliac crest at the end of a normal expiration.
5. Classify the result using the tables below.

## Observations and calculations

| Measurement | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight (kg) | |
| Height (cm) / (m) | |
| Height² (m²) | |
| BMI (kg/m²) | |
| Waist circumference (cm, optional) | |

**Worked example:** weight 68 kg, height 1.70 m → height² = 2.89 m² → BMI = 68 ÷ 2.89 = **23.5 kg/m²** — normal by WHO cut-offs but "overweight" by the Indian cut-offs.

| Category | WHO (international) BMI | Indian consensus (Asian Indians) BMI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Underweight | Below 18.5 | Below 18.0 |
| Normal | 18.5–24.9 | 18.0–22.9 |
| Overweight | 25.0–29.9 | 23.0–24.9 |
| Obese | 30.0 and above | 25.0 and above |

Waist circumference above about 90 cm in Indian men and 80 cm in Indian women suggests abdominal (central) obesity.

## Result

The BMI of the subject is ______ kg/m², which falls in the ______ category.

## Precautions

1. Calibrate the scale and place it on a flat, hard floor.
2. Measure without shoes and with light clothing.
3. Keep the head in a level position for height.
4. Remember BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis; it is not used in the same way for children, pregnant women and athletes.

## Viva questions

1. **Write the formula for BMI.** Weight in kg divided by the square of height in metres.
2. **What is a normal BMI by WHO standards?** 18.5–24.9 kg/m².
3. **Why are lower cut-offs used for Indians?** They have more body fat and a higher risk of diabetes and heart disease at the same BMI.
4. **Give one limitation of BMI.** It does not distinguish muscle from fat or show fat distribution.
5. **What does waist circumference indicate?** Abdominal (visceral) fat, a risk factor for diabetes and heart disease.
6. **Name a drug class that commonly causes weight gain.** Corticosteroids (also insulin, some antipsychotics).
practicals.title: Recording of body mass index (BMI)

# Study of family planning devices and pregnancy diagnosis test

**Aim:** (A) To study the common family planning (contraceptive) methods and devices. (B) To perform a urine pregnancy test using an hCG test strip or card.

## Principle

**Contraception** prevents pregnancy by stopping sperm from meeting the ovum (barrier methods, sterilisation), preventing ovulation (hormonal methods), or preventing fertilization and implantation in the uterus (intrauterine devices).

**Pregnancy test:** after implantation the trophoblast secretes **human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**, which appears in maternal blood and urine. Urine test cards use **immunochromatography**: urine flows along a strip carrying coloured antibody against hCG; if hCG is present, the coloured complex is captured by a second antibody at the **test line (T)**, while a **control line (C)** shows that the strip worked. Most cards become positive around the time of the first missed period; early-morning urine is the most concentrated.

## Requirements

**A.** Specimens, models or charts of: male and female condoms, diaphragm, copper intrauterine device (e.g. Copper T), a hormone-releasing intrauterine system, combined oral contraceptive pill pack, weekly non-steroidal pill (centchroman), emergency contraceptive pill pack, injectable contraceptive, implant (chart), charts of vasectomy and tubectomy.

**B.** Urine pregnancy test card with dropper, clean dry urine container, gloves, timer, sample of urine (a known positive control sample if available).

## Procedure

**A. Family planning devices**

1. Examine each device or pack and note its type, how it is used, how it works and its advantages and disadvantages.
2. Record the observations in the table below.

**B. Urine pregnancy test**

1. Wear gloves. Bring the card and urine to room temperature.
2. Remove the card from its pouch and place it on a flat surface.
3. Add the number of drops of urine stated by the manufacturer (usually 3) to the sample well (S).
4. Start the timer and read the result in the time given in the leaflet (usually about 5 minutes); do not read after the maximum time.

## Observations

**A. Contraceptive methods**

| Method | Examples | How it works | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Barrier** | Male condom, female condom, diaphragm with spermicide | Blocks sperm from entering the uterus | Condoms also protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV |
| **Intrauterine devices** | Copper T (copper IUD); levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system | Copper is toxic to sperm and makes the uterus unfavourable for implantation; hormonal device thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium | Long-acting and reversible; inserted by trained staff |
| **Combined oral pills** | Oestrogen + progestin daily (government supply: Mala-N) | Suppress FSH and LH → no ovulation; thick cervical mucus | Very effective if taken regularly; not for women with a history of clots |
| **Non-hormonal weekly pill** | Centchroman (ormeloxifene; Chhaya, earlier Saheli) | Selective oestrogen receptor modulator; prevents implantation | Developed in India; weekly dosing |
| **Emergency contraception** | Levonorgestrel pill | Delays or prevents ovulation | For occasional use after unprotected intercourse, as soon as possible (within 72 hours); not a regular method |
| **Injectable** | DMPA (Antara) | Progestin; prevents ovulation | Given every 3 months |
| **Implant** | Progestin rod under the skin of the arm | Prevents ovulation | Several years; removable |
| **Permanent (sterilisation)** | **Vasectomy** (vas deferens cut and tied) and **tubectomy** (uterine tubes cut, tied or blocked) | Stops sperm or ovum from passing | Permanent; vasectomy is simpler and safer |
| Natural | Calendar (safe period), withdrawal, lactational amenorrhoea | Avoid intercourse in the fertile days | Less reliable |

**B. Pregnancy test**

| Appearance | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| Line at C only | **Negative** — hCG not detected |
| Lines at both C and T (even a faint T line) | **Positive** — hCG detected |
| No line at C (with or without T) | **Invalid** — repeat with a new card |

## Result

(A) The common family planning devices and methods were studied. (B) The urine pregnancy test on the given sample was ______ (positive / negative).

## Precautions

1. Wear gloves when handling urine; dispose of samples and cards safely.
2. Check the expiry date of the card; do not reuse it.
3. Read the result only within the stated time.
4. A negative result very early in pregnancy may be false; repeat after a few days if periods do not start.
5. Handle contraceptive specimens respectfully and do not open sealed sterile packs.

## Viva questions

1. **Which hormone is detected in a pregnancy test?** Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG).
2. **What is the role of the control line?** It shows that the test card worked and enough sample was added.
3. **How does Copper T prevent pregnancy?** Copper ions are toxic to sperm and make the endometrium unfavourable for implantation.
4. **How do combined oral pills prevent pregnancy?** By suppressing FSH and the LH surge, so ovulation does not occur.
5. **Which contraceptive also protects against sexually transmitted infections?** The condom.
6. **What is vasectomy?** Cutting and tying of the vas deferens in men — a permanent method.

# Demonstration of total blood count by an automated cell analyser

**Aim:** To demonstrate the estimation of a complete blood count (CBC) using an automated haematology cell analyser and to interpret the report.

## Principle

Automated haematology analysers count and size thousands of cells in seconds, replacing the manual haemocytometer counts learnt in BP107P.

- **Electrical impedance (Coulter principle):** blood diluted in a conducting fluid is drawn through a tiny aperture across which a current flows. Each cell, being a poor conductor, briefly raises the resistance, giving a voltage pulse. The **number of pulses = number of cells**, and the **height of each pulse is proportional to cell volume**, so RBCs, WBCs and platelets are counted and sized.
- **Haemoglobin** is measured by photometry after the red cells are lysed (cyanide-free reagents such as sodium lauryl sulphate, or the cyanmethaemoglobin method).
- **WBC differential:** 3-part analysers separate lymphocytes, "mid" cells and granulocytes by size after a lysing reagent; 5-part analysers add **laser light scatter (flow cytometry)** and sometimes staining to separate neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils.
- From these measurements the analyser **calculates** haematocrit and the red cell indices.

## Requirements

Automated haematology analyser with its diluent, lyse and cleaning reagents; blood collected in an **EDTA (K2 or K3) tube** (purple/lavender cap); quality control blood; gloves, sharps container, printer.

## Procedure

1. Switch on the analyser; let it run its start-up checks and background count.
2. Run the manufacturer's **quality control** sample and confirm it is within range.
3. Collect venous blood into the EDTA tube to the marked level and mix gently by inverting 8–10 times (do not shake). Test within a few hours.
4. Enter the sample identity (patient number, age, sex).
5. Mix the tube again, remove the cap (or use closed-tube mode) and present the tube to the aspiration probe; press start.
6. The analyser aspirates a small volume, dilutes, lyses and counts automatically; read the printed report in about a minute.
7. Note any flags (e.g. abnormal cells, platelet clumps) that need a manual blood smear check.
8. Run the cleaning cycle and switch off as per the manual.

## Observations

| Parameter | Subject's value | Normal adult range (approximate) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RBC count | | 4.5–5.5 million/µL (men); 4.0–5.0 million/µL (women) |
| Haemoglobin | | 13–17 g/dL (men); 12–15 g/dL (women) |
| Haematocrit (PCV) | | 40–50% (men); 36–46% (women) |
| MCV | | 80–100 fL |
| MCH | | 27–32 pg |
| MCHC | | 32–36 g/dL |
| RDW | | about 11.5–14.5% |
| Total WBC count | | 4,000–11,000/µL |
| Neutrophils / lymphocytes / monocytes / eosinophils / basophils | | 40–75% / 20–40% / 2–10% / 1–6% / 0–1% |
| Platelet count | | 1.5–4.0 lakh/µL |

Normal ranges vary slightly between laboratories and analysers; use the ranges printed on the report.

**Red cell indices (calculated):**

- **MCV (fL) = (Hct % × 10) ÷ RBC (millions/µL)**
- **MCH (pg) = (Hb g/dL × 10) ÷ RBC (millions/µL)**
- **MCHC (g/dL) = (Hb ÷ Hct %) × 100**

**Worked example:** Hb 15 g/dL, RBC 5.0 million/µL, Hct 45% → MCV = 450 ÷ 5 = **90 fL**; MCH = 150 ÷ 5 = **30 pg**; MCHC = 15 ÷ 45 × 100 = **33.3 g/dL** — normocytic, normochromic.

**Interpretation:** low MCV and MCH → microcytic hypochromic anaemia (iron deficiency, thalassaemia); high MCV → macrocytic anaemia (vitamin B12 or folate deficiency); high WBC → infection or leukaemia; low platelets → bleeding risk.

## Result

The complete blood count of the given sample was obtained by the automated analyser: Hb ______ g/dL, RBC ______ million/µL, WBC ______ /µL, platelets ______ /µL; the picture is ______.

## Precautions

1. Treat all blood as potentially infectious: wear gloves, dispose of sharps safely.
2. Use the correct anticoagulant (EDTA), fill to the mark and mix gently; clotted or haemolysed samples give false results.
3. Run quality control before patient samples.
4. Follow the manufacturer's maintenance and cleaning schedule.
5. Confirm flagged results by examining a stained blood smear.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the Coulter principle?** Counting and sizing cells by the change in electrical impedance as each cell passes through a small aperture.
2. **Which anticoagulant is used for a CBC?** EDTA (K2 or K3), because it preserves cell shape.
3. **How is MCV calculated?** Haematocrit (%) × 10 ÷ RBC count (millions/µL).
4. **What does a low MCV suggest?** Microcytic anaemia, commonly iron deficiency.
5. **Give two advantages of automated counting over manual counting.** Speed and precision (thousands of cells counted), plus extra indices such as RDW and MPV.
6. **When must a manual smear be examined?** When the analyser flags abnormal or immature cells, platelet clumps or results outside limits.
practicals.title: Demonstration of total blood count by cell analyser

# Study of permanent slides of vital organs and gonads

**Aim:** To identify, under the compound microscope, permanent stained slides of vital organs (stomach, small intestine, liver, pancreas, lung, kidney, thyroid, adrenal) and gonads (testis, ovary), and to draw their microscopic structure.

## Principle

Permanent slides are thin sections of tissue fixed, embedded, cut and stained, usually with **haematoxylin and eosin (H and E)**: haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple and eosin stains cytoplasm and fibres pink. Each organ shows a typical pattern of cells and structures that allows it to be recognised. Slides are first viewed under low power to see the general plan, then under high power for details.

## Requirements

Compound microscope, permanent slides of the organs listed, lens paper, immersion oil (if oil immersion is used), drawing sheets and pencil.

## Procedure

1. Place the slide on the stage with the coverslip up; focus first with the **low-power (10×)** objective.
2. Scan the whole section to see its general layout.
3. Switch to **high power (40×)** to study cells and special features.
4. Identify the organ using the points in the table.
5. Draw a neat labelled diagram of the low-power view with a high-power inset.

## Observations: identification points

| Slide | Identifying features |
| --- | --- |
| **Stomach (fundus)** | Simple columnar mucous epithelium with **gastric pits**; long straight **gastric glands** filling the mucosa with pink **parietal cells** and bluish **chief cells**; thick muscularis with three layers |
| **Small intestine** | Finger-like **villi** lined by columnar cells with **goblet cells** and brush border; **crypts of Lieberkühn**; central lacteal; **Brunner's glands** in the submucosa (duodenum) or **Peyer's patches** (ileum) |
| **Liver** | Hexagonal **lobules** with a **central vein**; plates of hepatocytes radiating outwards; **sinusoids**; **portal triads** (hepatic artery, portal vein, bile duct) at the corners |
| **Pancreas** | Many serous **acini** with dark basal and pink apical (granular) cytoplasm; scattered pale **islets of Langerhans**; ducts; no gastric pits or villi |
| **Lung** | Many thin-walled **alveoli** giving a lace-like look; bronchioles with smooth muscle and no cartilage; bronchi with cartilage plates; blood vessels |
| **Kidney** | **Cortex** with round **glomeruli** in Bowman's capsules and cut convoluted tubules (PCT with brush border, pinker; DCT paler); **medulla** with straight tubules and collecting ducts |
| **Thyroid** | Round **follicles** of cuboidal cells filled with pink **colloid**; parafollicular (C) cells between follicles; rich capillaries |
| **Adrenal gland** | Capsule; cortex in three zones — **glomerulosa** (clusters), **fasciculata** (long cords of pale, lipid-filled cells), **reticularis** (network); central **medulla** with chromaffin cells and large veins |
| **Testis** | Thick **tunica albuginea**; many cut **seminiferous tubules** lined by germ cells at all stages (spermatogonia at the edge, sperm near the lumen) and **Sertoli cells**; clusters of **Leydig cells** between tubules |
| **Ovary** | Outer **cortex** with follicles at different stages (**primordial**, primary, secondary, **Graafian** with antrum), possibly **corpus luteum** (large pale luteal cells) or corpus albicans; inner vascular **medulla** |

```text
 TESTIS (low power)                     OVARY (low power)
  _______________________                _________________________
 | tunica albuginea      |              | germinal epithelium      |
 |  (O) (O) (O)  <- seminiferous        |  o  primordial follicles |
 |  (O) (O) (O)     tubules   |         |   (O) Graafian follicle  |
 |   ..Leydig cells..   |               |       with antrum        |
 |_______________________|              |  CORTEX | MEDULLA (vessels)|
                                        |_________________________|
```

## Result

The permanent slides of the given organs were identified on the basis of their characteristic features and their diagrams were drawn.

## Precautions

1. Always begin with low power; never lower the objective onto the slide while looking through the eyepiece.
2. Clean lenses only with lens paper.
3. Handle slides by the edges and return them to the box.
4. Draw what is seen, not a textbook picture.

## Viva questions

1. **Which stain is commonly used for permanent slides?** Haematoxylin and eosin.
2. **How do you tell the pancreas from a salivary gland?** The pancreas has pale islets of Langerhans between the acini.
3. **What fills the thyroid follicles?** Colloid (thyroglobulin).
4. **Which cells of the testis secrete testosterone?** Leydig (interstitial) cells.
5. **What is a Graafian follicle?** A mature ovarian follicle with a large fluid-filled antrum, ready to ovulate.
6. **Which zone of the adrenal cortex is the thickest?** The zona fasciculata.
7. **How is the liver lobule recognised?** By the central vein with radiating plates of hepatocytes and portal triads at the corners.
